basis: Brokskat mannili bread closely matches Sawi mēṇḍili and the maṇḍa/maṇḍaka food family; final ili is a derivative whose formation must remain distinct from the broad scum headword.
Brokskat kry breast matches the independent Shina kro/kṛo bosom set and krōḍá, with loss of intervocalic retroflex and central vowel realization to be checked source-aware.
Brokskat dut breast has the exact milk-word structure of dugdhá descendants and is a metonymic anatomical sense. It is not a second reflex of krōḍá, and sense transfer must be retained.
Ushojo phoṭalo broken matches Shina phuṭilo result adjectives in the sphuṭyati family. Final alo/ilo is a modern participial derivative, not the simple finite old input.
Ushojo retroflex ʐa brother directly matches northern Shina ẓa and the bhrā́tr̥ kinship family; no mora distinction is written in the short survey token.

Brokskat baayo brother has an ultimate bhrā́tr̥-family comparison, but SchmidtKaul2008p248 explicitly identifies it as a loan from an unidentified Indo-Aryan language. Preserve first-syllable stress as loan adaptation evidence.
Ushojo mẽṣ buffalo matches contracted mahiṣá-type buffalo forms across Shinaic. Masculine/feminine old accent variants and nasalization remain unresolved; the survey is unmarked for tone.

Brokskat daazis intransitive burn has the j/z outcome of a passive/inchoative dahyátē-type stem, contrasted in the same source with transitive daahis. This morphological pair is stronger evidence than the English burn label alone.
Brokskat daahis transitive burn contrasts with daazis intransitive and fits the dāhayati causative family. The final is belongs to modern verbal morphology and is not part of the old root.

Ushojo kukuri chicken agrees with the repeated k and final liquid of the kukkuṭá regional chicken family, with a feminine or derivative i formation. Possible borrowing and ṭ/r history remain explicit.
Ushojo marcake chilli matches Shina marcaki and marīca pepper derivatives. The American crop referent implies later name transfer, and the ke extension is part of the relevant modern formation.
Ushojo ṭukae cloth closely matches Shina ṭukei cloth in the ṭukk cut/piece family, with final vowel sequence rather than a simple single-vowel ending.

Brokskat azes and Ushojo aẓo cloud share the diagnostic a-plus-retroflex/ž outcome of abhrá with Shina aẓo. Brokskat es and Ushojo o are different nominal formations or cells; their final versus initial stress is retained.
Ushojo šidalo cold exactly matches Shina šidalo and the independently ila/ala-extended śītalá adjective family; medial short stress precedes the gender ending.

Brokskat goo and Ushojo gao cow belong securely to the inherited go/gāv cow paradigm. The precise accusative, plural or remodeled a-stem input is left open; the records are not assigned a unique old stem accent from surface shape alone.

Brokskat qoo crow matches the velar-initial long-vowel crow family kā́ka through loss of intervocalic k; compare independent local uvularization rather than assuming a Tibetan replacement from the gloss.
Brokskat rus cry matches the rō-/ru- cry root shared across Shinaic, with the recurring Brokskat citation s. It is a root-family link, not a reconstruction of the finite old accent.

Ushojo phwi daughter agrees with Palula pheei/phi daughter and the putrī́ family, distinct from duhitŕ̥ despite identical English gloss. Consonant-cluster loss and the vowel sequence require separate positional interpretation.
Brokskat nus daughter-in-law directly matches Shina nuuṣ and snuṣā́ with initial-cluster simplification. Unlike the misnumbered Strand bhooy token, its n/s segments independently support this family.
Brokskat suri day is the sun-family word also used for day in Shina; initial stress and final i are retained, and this is a semantic extension rather than a divasa reflex.
Ushojo dez day directly matches Shina dez/diiz and divasá-type day forms; the monosyllable is unmarked for tone.

Brokskat minis die is provisionally compared with mriyátē-derived mirij/mini stems, with a recurring citation is ending. The medial n correspondence needs verification, so exclude from strict old-accent prediction until resolved.
Brokskat šwaa and Ushojo šũ dog belong to the śvan/śuna dog paradigm with independently attested w/n stem variation and nasal loss. They must be kept distinct from the unrelated kuccura dog set.
Ushojo dar door exactly matches Shina dar and the dvar/dvāra doorway family; no modern tone is marked.
Brokskat saacii dream agrees with Shina sā̃c̣u and the reconstructed svāpra dream family, with palatal outcome and final derivative vowel. The svapna alternative remains a historical competitor.
Brokskat pis drink preserves the pi root and recurring citation s; it is a secure lexical root comparison but not a direct reflex of the reduplicated píbati citation cell.

Brokskat šuko dry matches the simple śúṣka adjective, whereas Ushojo šukalo independently adds al before o. Their initial versus medial stress is therefore compared as distinct formations, not random divergence in one suffixless stem.

Brokskat kani ear has an extra final i and final stress; Ushojo koon is a contracted monosyllable. Both share the diagnostic k/n ear stem of kárṇa, but the Brokskat ending must be identified before calling its stress an unexplained shift.
Brokskat kxus eat shares the kh/khw eating root with Shinaic khā́dati-family forms and the recurring Brokskat citation s; the root vowel and phonatory notation need source-specific treatment.

SchmidtKaul2008p247 identifies Brokskat thul egg as Kashmiri borrowing. The ultimate sthūla large/thick semantic derivation is retained as a regional comparison, not direct Shinaic accent inheritance.
Ushojo aṇḍo egg matches the āṇḍa egg family and its o-ending derivatives; final syllable stress is observed, while the exact masculine/derivative formation remains open.
Ushojo kino batiŋar eggplant is a black-plus-eggplant compound. The batiŋar component belongs to vātiṅgaṇa; the whole phrase has two stress marks and cannot enter single-word accent counts.
Brokskat a~ṣ and Ushojo aaṭh eight show the independently regular aṣṭa numeral cluster outcomes and final-vowel loss; neither supplies an explicit mora accent.
Brokskat as'toṣ eighteen agrees with the aṣṭā́daśa compound numeral in both components and contraction; the source explicitly stresses the final syllable.

Brokskat qudes and Ushojo agaš eleven preserve recognizable first-plus-ten compound material matching ḗkādaśa; Brokskat q onset and u need separate historical explanation, while initial versus final syllable stress is retained.
Brokskat eey ewe matches the independently linked older Brokskat ēi ewe under ávi and its feminine sheep stem. It is a vowel sequence rather than securely a doubled monophthong accent token.

Brokskat ac̣hii and Ushojo ɛṣiː eye match ákṣi/akṣī́ in the affricate cluster outcome and final i. Ushojo initial stress contrasts with final-vowel prominence in the other source; the singular/dual-derived input is deliberately left unresolved.
Ushojo mukh face directly matches múkha; the related múkhya10174 is an alternative derivation but not independently needed for the exact segmental form.
Ushojo dur far directly matches dūrá and its Shinaic cognates. Survey quantity/aspiration and absent tone marking remain source limitations.
Ushojo mẽ fat matches Kundal mɛ and Shina med/mẽ derivatives of mḗdas, with consonant loss and nasalization requiring a specific stem history.
